questions.stem: Choose the sentence that has the CORRECT question tag for the clause 'She hardly speaks in meetings'.

options.option_text: She hardly speaks in meetings, doesn't she?
She hardly speaks in meetings, does she?
She hardly speaks in meetings, isn't she?
She hardly speaks in meetings, hasn't she?

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Hardly' is a semi-negative adverb (like rarely, seldom, barely, scarcely). When the main clause contains such a word, it carries an implicit negative meaning, so the question tag must be POSITIVE ('does she?'). Option A ('doesn't she') is the classic trap — students treat 'hardly' as a neutral adverb and apply the standard affirmative-clause rule. Rule: Negative adverbs (hardly, rarely, seldom, barely) → positive question tag. Example applying the same rule: 'He barely eats anything, does he?' — the positive tag 'does he' is mandatory here too.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correctly formed FIRST conditional sentence?

options.option_text: If it will rain, we shall cancel the match and go home early
If it rains, we shall cancel the match and go home early
If it rained, we shall cancel the match and go home early
If it rains, we would cancel the match and go home early

questions.explanation: B is correct. First conditional (real/possible future) rule: if-clause = Simple Present tense; main clause = will/shall + base verb. Option A is the most common error — 'will' must NEVER appear in the if-clause of a first conditional ('If it will rain' is wrong). Option C uses 'rained' (simple past), which belongs to the second conditional. Option D uses 'would', which signals a second conditional (unreal present). Rule summary: If + V1 (present), will/shall + V1. Example: 'If you study hard, you will pass.' — same structure.

questions.stem: Which sentence is grammatically CORRECT in the SECOND conditional?

options.option_text: If I was rich, I would travel across all seven continents of the world
If I were rich, I would travel across all seven continents of the world
If I were rich, I will travel across all seven continents of the world
If I am rich, I would travel across all seven continents of the world

questions.explanation: B is correct. Second conditional (unreal present/hypothetical) rule: if-clause uses PAST SUBJUNCTIVE 'were' for ALL persons (including 'I'), and the main clause uses would/could/might + base verb. Option A ('was') is colloquially used but is marked incorrect in SSC/bank exams, which test formal grammar where 'were' is mandatory for the subjunctive mood. Option C uses 'will' (future, real) instead of 'would' (hypothetical), making it a first conditional error. Option D uses simple present 'am', treating the condition as factual rather than unreal. Example: 'If he were the director, he would revamp the policy.' — 'were' is required even for third person singular.

questions.stem: If the medicine ___ on time, the patient would not have deteriorated so rapidly.

options.option_text: had arrived — past perfect correctly used in third conditional
arrived — simple past tense used without perfective aspect
would have arrived — modal perfect incorrectly placed in if-clause
has arrived — present perfect incorrectly used in if-clause

questions.explanation: A is correct. Third conditional (unreal past) rule: if-clause = Past Perfect (had + V3); main clause = would/could/might + have + V3. 'Had arrived' is the correct past perfect form. Option C ('would have arrived') is the most tempting error — 'would have' belongs only in the MAIN clause, never in the if-clause of any conditional. Option B ('arrived') is simple past, which belongs in second conditional if-clauses expressing unreal present. Option D ('has arrived') is present perfect, which has no role in conditional structures. Example applying the rule: 'If they had left earlier, they would have caught the flight.' — same pattern.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which 'unless' is used INCORRECTLY.

options.option_text: Unless you apologise, she will not forgive you for the mistake
Unless he doesn't study harder, he will fail the final examination
Unless it rains, the festival will be held outdoors as planned
Unless you confirm your attendance, your seat will be cancelled

questions.explanation: B is incorrect. 'Unless' already carries the meaning 'if...not', so pairing it with a negative verb ('doesn't') creates a double negative: 'Unless he doesn't study harder' = 'If he does not not study harder' — which reverses the intended meaning entirely. The correct form is: 'Unless he studies harder, he will fail.' Rule: Unless + affirmative verb = if + negative verb. Options A, C, and D are all correct — each uses an affirmative verb after 'unless', preserving the negative conditional logic. Example: 'Unless you hurry (= if you do not hurry), you will miss the train.' — note the affirmative 'hurry' after 'unless'.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is a MIXED conditional expressing an unreal past cause with a present consequence?

options.option_text: If she had joined the army, she would be a colonel by now
If she had joined the army, she would have been a colonel now
If she joined the army, she would be a colonel by now
If she joins the army, she will be a colonel in the future

questions.explanation: A is correct. A mixed conditional combines: Past Perfect in the if-clause (unreal PAST cause: 'had joined') + 'would + base verb' in the main clause (PRESENT consequence: 'would be a colonel by now'). Option B is pure third conditional — 'would have been' signals a PAST result, not a present one; the time-marker 'now' does not change its grammatical class. Option C is pure second conditional ('if she joined' = unreal present, not unreal past). Option D is a first conditional (real future). The diagnostic signal: if-clause has Past Perfect AND main clause has 'would + base verb' (not 'would have'), the sentence is a mixed conditional. Example: 'If he had exercised regularly, he would be fit today.' — same structure.

questions.stem: Identify the grammatically CORRECT inverted conditional (where 'if' has been dropped and the auxiliary fronted).

options.option_text: Were she to invest wisely, she would double her returns within a year
Was she to invest wisely, she would double her returns within a year
Were she to invest wisely, she will double her returns within a year
Should she to invest wisely, she would double her returns within a year

questions.explanation: A is correct. Inverted conditionals omit 'if' and front the auxiliary. For a second conditional subjunctive ('If she were to invest'), the inversion uses 'Were + subject + to + base verb': 'Were she to invest wisely, she would...' — 'were' is mandatory regardless of person or number. Option B ('Was she to') fails because 'was' can NEVER replace 'were' in subjunctive inversion; the subjunctive form 'were' is the only acceptable auxiliary here. Option C ('she will') switches the main clause to future tense, converting a second conditional (hypothetical) into a first conditional (real future) — structurally inconsistent. Option D ('Should she to') is doubly wrong: 'should' is used to invert first conditionals ('Should it rain, we will cancel'), and 'should' inversion NEVER takes 'to' after it ('Should she invest', not 'Should she to invest'). Example: 'Were I the CEO, I would overhaul the process.' — same inversion pattern.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences has the CORRECT question tag attached to an imperative clause?

options.option_text: Come here right now, don't you?
Post this letter today, will you?
Sit down quietly at once, are you?
Help me carry this bag, shall they?

questions.explanation: B is correct. Rule: Imperative sentences (commands or requests) take 'will you?' as the standard question tag, or 'won't you?' for a more polite tone. Option A ('don't you?') is the negative tag for positive declarative sentences, not for imperatives. Option C ('are you?') is not a valid question-tag form in any standard sentence pattern. Option D ('shall they?') uses the wrong subject pronoun — the implied subject in an imperative is always 'you,' never 'they.' Another example applying the same rule: 'Bring me the file, will you?'

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correctly formed ZERO CONDITIONAL sentence?

options.option_text: If water reaches 100°C, it boils and turns into vapour
If water reaches 100°C, it will boil and turn into vapour
If water reached 100°C, it would boil and turn into vapour
If water had reached 100°C, it would have boiled into vapour

questions.explanation: A is correct. The zero conditional expresses universal truths and scientific facts using the structure: If + present simple, present simple. Option B ('will boil') converts the sentence into a first conditional, which expresses a real future possibility. Option C ('would boil') produces a second conditional, expressing a hypothetical present situation. Option D ('would have boiled') creates a third conditional, which describes an unreal past situation. Rule: Zero conditional = If + V1, V1 — both clauses in the present simple. Another example: 'If you freeze water, it becomes ice.'

questions.stem: Choose the correct question tag to complete: 'Nothing can stop us from achieving our goal, ___'

options.option_text: can they, since 'us' in the main clause needs a plural tag
cannot it, since negative clauses need a negative question tag
can it, since 'nothing' is singular and the clause is negative
can we, since the speaker is part of 'us' stated in the clause

questions.explanation: C is correct. Two rules apply together here. (1) The tag pronoun must agree with the grammatical subject of the main clause — the subject is 'nothing,' which is singular and takes 'it,' not 'they' or 'we.' (2) 'Nothing' is an inherently negative indefinite pronoun (equivalent to 'not anything'), so the clause is already negative and the tag must be positive: 'can it?' Option A ('can they?') wrongly references 'us' as the tag subject instead of 'nothing.' Option B ('cannot it?') creates a forbidden double-negative tag — a negative clause always takes a positive tag. Option D ('can we?') substitutes the speaker for the grammatical subject. Another example: 'Nobody called, did they?' — 'nobody' is negative, so the tag is positive.

questions.stem: Choose the conditional conjunction that best fills the blank: 'You may borrow my notes ___ you return them before the deadline.'

options.option_text: unless, which introduces a negative exception to the permission
provided that, which sets a positive condition for the action
in case, which expresses a precautionary preparatory action
even if, which signals that the condition does not affect the result

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Provided that' means 'on the condition that' and introduces a positive requirement that must be satisfied. Option A ('unless') means 'if not,' so 'You may borrow unless you return them' inverts the intended meaning — it would allow borrowing only if the notes are NOT returned. Option C ('in case') expresses precautionary readiness for a possible future event (e.g., 'Take an umbrella in case it rains'), not a condition of permission. Option D ('even if') signals that the main clause holds regardless of the condition, making the borrowing unconditional — again wrong. Rule: 'provided that' = 'if and only if,' making it the correct marker for a positive enabling condition. Another example: 'She will participate provided that her registration is confirmed.'

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences correctly uses a question tag after a 'LET'S' construction?

options.option_text: Let's plan a surprise party for her, will we?
Let's plan a surprise party for her, don't we?
Let's plan a surprise party for her, should we?
Let's plan a surprise party for her, shall we?

questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Let's' (a contraction of 'let us') makes a first-person plural suggestion or proposal. Rule: 'Let's + base verb' always takes the tag 'shall we?' — this is the ONLY standard question tag for 'Let's' constructions in modern English grammar. Option A ('will we?') is used for imperatives directed at 'you,' not for 'Let's' proposals. Option B ('don't we?') is a declarative-negative tag and has no grammatical basis after a 'Let's' clause. Option C ('should we?') is not a valid question-tag form; 'should' belongs to conditional and advisory clauses, not tags. Mnemonic: Let's → shall we? Another example applying this rule: 'Let's take a short break, shall we?'

questions.stem: Which option correctly completes the question tag: 'He used to walk five kilometres every morning in his youth, ___'

options.option_text: usedn't he, applying the auxiliary-based tag rule strictly
didn't he, treating 'used to' as an ordinary past-tense verb
wouldn't he, since 'used to' describes a habitual past action
hadn't he, as 'used to' is equivalent to the past perfect tense

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Used to' is a semi-modal expressing past habit or state. In modern standard English, question tags for 'used to' treat it as a full lexical verb in the simple past; therefore the tag is formed with 'did/didn't + subject pronoun.' Rule: 'used to' → tag with 'did/didn't.' Option A ('usedn't he?') is the historically formal tag that treated 'used' as a true auxiliary — it is archaic and non-standard in contemporary exam English, and most modern grammar authorities do not accept it. Option C ('wouldn't he?') confuses 'used to' (stating a past habitual fact) with the conditional modal 'would' (hypothetical). Option D ('hadn't he?') incorrectly assigns past-perfect auxiliary status to 'used to,' which is never classed as a perfect-aspect verb. Another example: 'She used to live in Mysore, didn't she?'

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses 'wish' to express regret about a CURRENT (present) situation?

options.option_text: I wish I know the right answer to solve this problem now
I wish I had known the right answer to solve this problem now
I wish I knew the right answer to solve this problem now
I wish I would know the right answer to solve this problem now

questions.explanation: C is correct. To express a wish or regret about a PRESENT or ongoing situation, English uses: wish + past simple (subjunctive). 'Knew' is the past simple of 'know,' signalling an unreal hypothetical present condition. Option A ('wish I know') uses the simple present after 'wish,' which is grammatically incorrect in hypothetical wish constructions. Option B ('wish I had known') uses past perfect — this structure is reserved for regret about a PAST event that cannot be undone (e.g., 'I wish I had studied harder last year'); the marker 'now' in the sentence creates a direct tense conflict with 'had known,' making it wrong here. Option D ('wish I would know') is incorrect because 'would' after 'wish' is only used to express a desire for someone else's behaviour to change (e.g., 'I wish he would stop interrupting'), never for the speaker's own present state or ability. Rule: Wish + past simple = present/future hypothetical regret; Wish + past perfect = past regret. Another example: 'I wish I spoke French fluently' (present hypothetical regret).'
